claim: Autophagy is a catabolic process for bulk degradation of cytosolic materials mediated by double-membraned autophagosomes.
source: Autophagy is a catabolic process for bulk degradation of cytosolic materials mediated by double-membraned autophagosomes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about autophagy that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A cell-free assay based on LC3 lipidation can define the organelle membrane supporting early autophagosome formation.
source: Here, we establish a cell-free assay based on LC3 lipidation to define the organelle membrane supporting early autophagosome formation.
evidence: The authors describe establishing this assay as part of their experimental approach.

claim: In vitro LC3 lipidation requires energy.
source: In vitro LC3 lipidation requires energy and is subject to regulation by the pathways modulating autophagy in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating ATP dependence.

claim: In vitro LC3 lipidation is subject to regulation by the pathways modulating autophagy in vivo.
source: In vitro LC3 lipidation requires energy and is subject to regulation by the pathways modulating autophagy in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data showing effects of starvation, PI3K inhibitors, and other regulatory factors on the in vitro system.

claim: The ERGIC is a primary membrane source necessary to trigger LC3 lipidation in vitro.
source: We developed a systematic membrane isolation scheme to identify the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) as a primary membrane source both necessary and sufficient to trigger LC3 lipidation in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by membrane fractionation data in Figures 4-8 showing ERGIC enrichment correlates with lipidation activity.

claim: The ERGIC is sufficient to trigger LC3 lipidation in vitro.
source: We developed a systematic membrane isolation scheme to identify the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) as a primary membrane source both necessary and sufficient to trigger LC3 lipidation in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoisolation experiments in Figure 8B,C showing ERGIC-positive membranes have enhanced lipidation activity.

claim: The ERGIC is required for autophagosome biogenesis in vivo.
source: Functional studies demonstrate that the ERGIC is required for autophagosome biogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 9-10 showing that disruption of ERGIC with drugs or genetic manipulations inhibits LC3 puncta formation.

claim: The ERGIC acts by recruiting the early autophagosome marker ATG14.
source: Moreover, we find that the ERGIC acts by recruiting the early autophagosome marker ATG14, a critical step for the generation of preautophagosomal membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 11-12 showing that ERGIC disruption prevents ATG14 recruitment and that ATG14 colocalizes with ERGIC markers.

claim: Autophagy allows cells to cope with stresses such as starvation, hypoxia, and pathogen infection.
source: Autophagy also allows cells to cope with stresses such as starvation, hypoxia, and pathogen infection (Mizushima et al., 2008; Burman and Ktistakis, 2010; Levine, 2005; Yang and Klionsky, 2010; Weidberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Starvation-induced autophagy involves inhibition of MTOR.
source: In the process of starvation-induced autophagy, several upstream signals are triggered, including inhibition of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (MTOR), and activation of the Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and AMP kinase (AMPK) (Noda and Ohsumi, 1998; Wei et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2011; Rubinsztein et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations describing the regulatory pathways of autophagy.

claim: Starvation-induced autophagy involves activation of JNK.
source: In the process of starvation-induced autophagy, several upstream signals are triggered, including inhibition of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (MTOR), and activation of the Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and AMP kinase (AMPK) (Noda and Ohsumi, 1998; Wei et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2011; Rubinsztein et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations describing the regulatory pathways of autophagy.

claim: Starvation-induced autophagy involves activation of AMPK.
source: In the process of starvation-induced autophagy, several upstream signals are triggered, including inhibition of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (MTOR), and activation of the Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and AMP kinase (AMPK) (Noda and Ohsumi, 1998; Wei et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2011; Rubinsztein et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations describing the regulatory pathways of autophagy.

claim: Cells lacking ATG5 are deficient in starvation-induced autophagy and phagophore formation.
source: Cells lacking ATG5 are deficient in starvation-induced autophagy and phagophore formation (Mizushima et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and is used as the basis for using Atg5 KO cells in the experimental system.

claim: Atg5 KO cells only contain unmodified LC3 (LC3-I) in both cytosol and membrane fractions.
source: Hence they only contain unmodified LC3 (LC3-I) in both cytosol and membrane fractions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 1A showing only LC3-I in Atg5 KO MEF fractions.

claim: Cytosols derived from WT cells are highly enriched in LC3-I.
source: Cytosols derived from WT cells (including WT MEF [mouse embryonic fibroblast], COS-7 [Cercopithecus aethiops fibroblast-like kidney cells], and HEK293T [human embryonic kidney 293T cells]) were highly enriched in LC3-I whereas the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) sedimented with membranes (Kabeya et al., 2000 and Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1A and supported by a literature citation.

claim: LC3-II sediments with membranes in WT cells.
source: Cytosols derived from WT cells (including WT MEF [mouse embryonic fibroblast], COS-7 [Cercopithecus aethiops fibroblast-like kidney cells], and HEK293T [human embryonic kidney 293T cells]) were highly enriched in LC3-I whereas the lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) sedimented with membranes (Kabeya et al., 2000 and Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1A and supported by a literature citation.

claim: In vitro LC3 lipidation occurs in a time-dependent manner.
source: We incubated membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs with cytosol from WT MEFs in the presence of GTP and an ATP regeneration system (Figure 1B) and observed the formation of LC3-II in a time- (Figure 1B) and ATP-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In vitro LC3 lipidation is ATP-dependent.
source: We incubated membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs with cytosol from WT MEFs in the presence of GTP and an ATP regeneration system (Figure 1B) and observed the formation of LC3-II in a time- (Figure 1B) and ATP-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiment in Figure 1C showing reduced lipidation without ATP.

claim: In vitro-generated LC3-II partitions in the 16,000×g membrane fraction.
source: In a crude fractionation study, we found that the in vitro-generated LC3-II partitioned in the 16,000×g membrane fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by fractionation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In vitro-generated LC3-II resists extraction with urea.
source: Moreover, the in vitro product resisted extraction with urea or Na2CO3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and was delipidated to LC3-I by ATG4B (Figure 1D), a cysteine protease that cleaves the C-terminal tail of LC3 and removes PE from LC3-II (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the biochemical extraction experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In vitro-generated LC3-II resists extraction with Na2CO3.
source: Moreover, the in vitro product resisted extraction with urea or Na2CO3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and was delipidated to LC3-I by ATG4B (Figure 1D), a cysteine protease that cleaves the C-terminal tail of LC3 and removes PE from LC3-II (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the biochemical extraction experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In vitro-generated LC3-II is delipidated to LC3-I by ATG4B.
source: Moreover, the in vitro product resisted extraction with urea or Na2CO3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and was delipidated to LC3-I by ATG4B (Figure 1D), a cysteine protease that cleaves the C-terminal tail of LC3 and removes PE from LC3-II (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ATG4B treatment experiment in Figure 1D.

claim: ATG4B is a cysteine protease that cleaves the C-terminal tail of LC3 and removes PE from LC3-II.
source: Moreover, the in vitro product resisted extraction with urea or Na2CO3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and was delipidated to LC3-I by ATG4B (Figure 1D), a cysteine protease that cleaves the C-terminal tail of LC3 and removes PE from LC3-II (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATG4B function supported by a literature citation.

claim: Starvation-induced lipidation of LC3 requires the ATG12–ATG5 conjugate.
source: Starvation-induced lipidation of LC3 requires the ATG12–ATG5 conjugate (Mizushima et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: LC3-II formation is stimulated about threefold by cytosol and membranes from starved WT MEFs compared to non-starved MEFs.
source: LC3-II formation was stimulated about threefold in incubations containing cytosol from starved WT MEFs and membranes from starved Atg5 KO MEFs, compared to incubations containing cytosol and membranes from non-starved MEFs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cytosol from Atg5 KO MEFs does not generate LC3-II when combined with membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs.
source: Cytosol from Atg5 KO MEFs did not generate LC3-II when combined with membranes from Atg5 KO MEFs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by the immunoblot data in Figure 2A.

claim: Cytosols from COS-7 and HEK293T cells reconstitute starvation-induced lipidation of LC3.
source: In addition, cytosols from COS-7 and HEK293T cells also reconstituted starvation-induced lipidation of LC3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell-free LC3 lipidation is regulated by starvation-induced components in cells.
source: These data suggest that the cell-free LC3 lipidation is regulated by starvation-induced components in cells and is dependent on ATG5.
evidence: This is inferred from the starvation-dependent enhancement of lipidation shown in Figure 2A and related experiments.

claim: Cell-free LC3 lipidation is dependent on ATG5.
source: These data suggest that the cell-free LC3 lipidation is regulated by starvation-induced components in cells and is dependent on ATG5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of lipidation with Atg5 KO cytosol shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Starvation-induced autophagosome biogenesis requires the class III PI3K complex.
source: Starvation-induced autophagosome biogenesis requires the class III PI3K complex which contains ATG14, BECN1, VPS15, and the PI3K subunit VPS34 (Burman and Ktistakis, 2010; Obara and Ohsumi, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: The class III PI3K complex contains ATG14, BECN1, VPS15, and VPS34.
source: Starvation-induced autophagosome biogenesis requires the class III PI3K complex which contains ATG14, BECN1, VPS15, and the PI3K subunit VPS34 (Burman and Ktistakis, 2010; Obara and Ohsumi, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the PI3K complex supported by literature citations.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K activity prevents autophagy.
source: Inhibition of the PI3K activity prevents autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the autophagy field.

claim: LC3 lipidation is inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by 3-methyladenine.
source: LC3 lipidation was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by 3-methyladenine (3-MA) and wortmannin, two PI3K inhibitors of different potency but which act in the same concentration ranges to block autophagy in intact cells (Figure 2B and Klionsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 2B.

claim: LC3 lipidation is inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by wortmannin.
source: LC3 lipidation was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by 3-methyladenine (3-MA) and wortmannin, two PI3K inhibitors of different potency but which act in the same concentration ranges to block autophagy in intact cells (Figure 2B and Klionsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 2B.

claim: 3-methyladenine and wortmannin are PI3K inhibitors that act in the same concentration ranges to block autophagy in intact cells.
source: LC3 lipidation was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner by 3-methyladenine (3-MA) and wortmannin, two PI3K inhibitors of different potency but which act in the same concentration ranges to block autophagy in intact cells (Figure 2B and Klionsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: The FYVE domain binds to PI3P.
source: The FYVE domain binds to PI3P (Stenmark and Aasland, 1999) and when expressed in excess blocks autophagy in the cell by sequestering PI3P (Axe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: FYVE domain expressed in excess blocks autophagy in the cell by sequestering PI3P.
source: The FYVE domain binds to PI3P (Stenmark and Aasland, 1999) and when expressed in excess blocks autophagy in the cell by sequestering PI3P (Axe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: FYVE domain peptide inhibits LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As reported in intact cells, the FYVE domain peptide inhibited LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner whereas a cysteine to serine (C/S) mutation, which abolishes the ability of FYVE to bind PI3P (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C and Axe et al., 2008), had no effect on lipidation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 2C.

claim: A cysteine to serine (C/S) mutation in FYVE abolishes the ability of FYVE to bind PI3P.
source: As reported in intact cells, the FYVE domain peptide inhibited LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner whereas a cysteine to serine (C/S) mutation, which abolishes the ability of FYVE to bind PI3P (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C and Axe et al., 2008), had no effect on lipidation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PIP strip blot in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and supported by a literature citation.

claim: FYVE (C/S) mutation has no effect on LC3 lipidation.
source: As reported in intact cells, the FYVE domain peptide inhibited LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner whereas a cysteine to serine (C/S) mutation, which abolishes the ability of FYVE to bind PI3P (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C and Axe et al., 2008), had no effect on lipidation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2C showing no inhibition with FYVE (C/S).

claim: LC3 is synthesized as a precursor that is processed by ATG4 cleavage to expose a glycine at position 120.
source: LC3 is synthesized as a precursor that is processed by ATG4 cleavage to expose a glycine at position 120, the site of PE attachment (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LC3 processing supported by a literature citation.

claim: Glycine at position 120 of LC3 is the site of PE attachment.
source: LC3 is synthesized as a precursor that is processed by ATG4 cleavage to expose a glycine at position 120, the site of PE attachment (Tanida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 (aa1-120) requires the glycine at position 120.
source: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 (aa1-120) required the glycine at position 120 and responded in a cytosol- and membrane concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of wild-type and G/A mutant in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 responds in a cytosol concentration-dependent manner.
source: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 (aa1-120) required the glycine at position 120 and responded in a cytosol- and membrane concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the titration data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 responds in a membrane concentration-dependent manner.
source: Cell-free lipidation of recombinant T7-LC3 (aa1-120) required the glycine at position 120 and responded in a cytosol- and membrane concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the titration data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lipidated T7-LC3 sediments along with membranes at 16,000×g.
source: Lipidated T7-LC3 sedimented along with membranes at 16,000×g, a property shared with the endogenous LC3-II generated in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Figure1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fractionation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cytosol and membranes isolated from starved cells stimulate T7-LC3 lipidation in vitro.
source: Cytosol and membranes isolated from starved cells stimulated T7-LC3 lipidation in vitro (Figure 3A), just as we observed with endogenous LC3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3A.

claim: PI3K inhibitors 3-MA and wortmannin block in vitro T7-LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Likewise, PI3K inhibitors, 3-MA and wortmannin, and the PI3P blocking peptide, FYVE, blocked in vitro T7-LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3B.

claim: FYVE peptide blocks in vitro T7-LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Likewise, PI3K inhibitors, 3-MA and wortmannin, and the PI3P blocking peptide, FYVE, blocked in vitro T7-LC3 lipidation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: Cytosol deficient in ATG7 fails to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro.
source: Furthermore, cytosol deficient in ATG7, ATG3 or ATG5, key factors in the ubiquitin-like pathway for LC3 lipidation, failed to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro (Figure 3D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3F showing no lipidation with Atg7 KO cytosol.

claim: Cytosol deficient in ATG3 fails to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro.
source: Furthermore, cytosol deficient in ATG7, ATG3 or ATG5, key factors in the ubiquitin-like pathway for LC3 lipidation, failed to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro (Figure 3D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3E showing no lipidation with Atg3 KO cytosol.

claim: Cytosol deficient in ATG5 fails to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro.
source: Furthermore, cytosol deficient in ATG7, ATG3 or ATG5, key factors in the ubiquitin-like pathway for LC3 lipidation, failed to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro (Figure 3D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3D showing no lipidation with Atg5 KO cytosol.

claim: ATG7, ATG3, and ATG5 are key factors in the ubiquitin-like pathway for LC3 lipidation.
source: Furthermore, cytosol deficient in ATG7, ATG3 or ATG5, key factors in the ubiquitin-like pathway for LC3 lipidation, failed to generate lipidated T7-LC3 in vitro (Figure 3D,E and F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the LC3 lipidation machinery.

claim: Cytosol from starved or untreated Ulk1 KO MEFs reduces lipidation two to threefold relative to cytosol from WT cells.
source: We found that cytosol from starved or untreated Ulk1 KO MEFs reduced lipidation two to threefold relative to cytosol from WT cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative comparison in Figure 3G.

claim: T7-LC3 lipidation is stimulated two to threefold by rapamycin.
source: Furthermore, T7-LC3 lipidation was stimulated two to threefold by two MTOR inhibitors, rapamycin (Heitman et al., 1991) and Torin 1 (Liu et al., 2010), known to induce autophagy (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative data in Figure 3H.

claim: T7-LC3 lipidation is stimulated two to threefold by Torin 1.
source: Furthermore, T7-LC3 lipidation was stimulated two to threefold by two MTOR inhibitors, rapamycin (Heitman et al., 1991) and Torin 1 (Liu et al., 2010), known to induce autophagy (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative data in Figure 3I.

claim: Rapamycin is an MTOR inhibitor known to induce autophagy.
source: Furthermore, T7-LC3 lipidation was stimulated two to threefold by two MTOR inhibitors, rapamycin (Heitman et al., 1991) and Torin 1 (Liu et al., 2010), known to induce autophagy (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: Torin 1 is an MTOR inhibitor known to induce autophagy.
source: Furthermore, T7-LC3 lipidation was stimulated two to threefold by two MTOR inhibitors, rapamycin (Heitman et al., 1991) and Torin 1 (Liu et al., 2010), known to induce autophagy (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: The 25k pellet contains most (>70%) of the total LC3 lipidation activity.
source: The 25k pellet contained most (>70%) of the total activity, whereas the 100k pellet had little (<10%) total activity due to low levels of membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: The 100k pellet has little (<10%) total LC3 lipidation activity due to low levels of membrane.
source: The 25k pellet contained most (>70%) of the total activity, whereas the 100k pellet had little (<10%) total activity due to low levels of membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: The 25k membrane is enriched in peroxisomes (PMP70/ABCD3).
source: The 25k membrane was enriched in peroxisomes (PMP70/ABCD3), late endosomes (LAMP2) and cis-Golgi (GM130/GOLGA2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The 25k membrane is enriched in late endosomes (LAMP2).
source: The 25k membrane was enriched in peroxisomes (PMP70/ABCD3), late endosomes (LAMP2) and cis-Golgi (GM130/GOLGA2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The 25k membrane is enriched in cis-Golgi (GM130/GOLGA2).
source: The 25k membrane was enriched in peroxisomes (PMP70/ABCD3), late endosomes (LAMP2) and cis-Golgi (GM130/GOLGA2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The 25k membrane contains membranes from the ERGIC (SEC22B and ERGIC53/LMAN1).
source: This fraction also contained membranes from the ERGIC (SEC22B and ERGIC53/LMAN1), plasma membrane/early endosomes (PM/Endo, TFR), ER (RPN1), ER exit sites (ERES, active sites on the ER that generate COPII-coated vesicles, SEC12), lysosomes (Cathepsin D), and ATG9 vesicles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The lipidation activity is almost exclusively retained in the L fraction from sucrose gradient separation.
source: Interestingly, the lipidation activity was almost exclusively retained in the L fraction, which was enriched in ERGIC, cis-Golgi, ATG9 vesicles and plasma membrane/early endosomes (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activity measurements in Figure 6B and D.

claim: The L fraction is enriched in ERGIC, cis-Golgi, ATG9 vesicles and plasma membrane/early endosomes.
source: Interestingly, the lipidation activity was almost exclusively retained in the L fraction, which was enriched in ERGIC, cis-Golgi, ATG9 vesicles and plasma membrane/early endosomes (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: The P fraction mainly consists of ER, ERES, mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes.
source: In contrast, the P fraction, which mainly consisted of ER, ERES, mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes, induced very little T7-LC3 lipidation (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: The P fraction induces very little T7-LC3 lipidation.
source: In contrast, the P fraction, which mainly consisted of ER, ERES, mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes, induced very little T7-LC3 lipidation (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activity measurements in Figure 6B and D.

claim: The lipidation activity in OptiPrep gradient fractionation is distributed in fractions two through four which co-distribute with SEC22B and ERGIC53.
source: The lipidation activity was distributed in fractions two through four which co-distributed with SEC22B and ERGIC53 (Figure 7), two ERGIC markers (Zhang et al., 1999; Appenzeller-Herzog and Hauri, 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-distribution shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: SEC22B and ERGIC53 are ERGIC markers.
source: The lipidation activity was distributed in fractions two through four which co-distributed with SEC22B and ERGIC53 (Figure 7), two ERGIC markers (Zhang et al., 1999; Appenzeller-Herzog and Hauri, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: PE is not enriched in the fractions that trigger T7-LC3 lipidation.
source: Intriguingly, PE, the substrate for LC3 lipidation, was not enriched in the fractions that triggered T7-LC3 lipidation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PE measurements shown in the heat map in Figure 7B.

claim: The high activity of ERGIC-enriched membrane fractions is not caused by selective enrichment of autophagic factors directly contributing to LC3 lipidation.
source: The high activity of these membrane fractions was not caused by selective enrichment of the autophagic factors directly contributing to LC3 lipidation, as all of these factors are enriched in the cytosol, or by influencing the formation of the ATG5–12–16 complex essential for LC3 lipidation (Fujita et al., 2008) compared with other membrane fractions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Factors other than those directly involved in catalyzing LC3 lipidation contribute to the high lipidation activity of ERGIC-enriched membranes.
source: These data indicate that factors other than those directly involved in catalyzing LC3 lipidation contribute to the high lipidation activity of these membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that autophagic factors are not enriched in the active fractions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The lipidation reaction triggered by ERGIC-enriched membranes is enhanced by cytosol from starved cells.
source: We further found that the lipidation reaction triggered by the ERGIC-enriched membranes was enhanced by cytosol from starved cells and was inhibited by wortmannin and FYVE peptide (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The lipidation reaction triggered by ERGIC-enriched membranes is inhibited by wortmannin.
source: We further found that the lipidation reaction triggered by the ERGIC-enriched membranes was enhanced by cytosol from starved cells and was inhibited by wortmannin and FYVE peptide (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The lipidation reaction triggered by ERGIC-enriched membranes is inhibited by FYVE peptide.
source: We further found that the lipidation reaction triggered by the ERGIC-enriched membranes was enhanced by cytosol from starved cells and was inhibited by wortmannin and FYVE peptide (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The lipidation activity of isolated ERGIC-enriched membranes is controlled by pathways that regulate autophagy in vivo.
source: These data suggest that the lipidation activity of the isolated membranes is controlled by the pathway(s) that regulate autophagy in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the starvation enhancement and inhibitor sensitivity shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Immunodepletion of ERGIC from the L fraction reduces the ability to induce T7-LC3 lipidation more than threefold.
source: After immunodepletion, both SEC22B and ERGIC53 membranes were reduced, whereas the plasma membrane/endosome membranes, indicated by transferrin receptor, were not affected. Significantly, the ability of the L fraction to induce T7-LC3 lipidation was reduced more than threefold (Figure 8A), suggesting that ERGIC contributes to the high activity of LC3 lipidation in the L fraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative comparison in Figure 8A.

claim: ERGIC contributes to the high activity of LC3 lipidation in the L fraction.
source: After immunodepletion, both SEC22B and ERGIC53 membranes were reduced, whereas the plasma membrane/endosome membranes, indicated by transferrin receptor, were not affected. Significantly, the ability of the L fraction to induce T7-LC3 lipidation was reduced more than threefold (Figure 8A), suggesting that ERGIC contributes to the high activity of LC3 lipidation in the L fraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunodepletion experiment showing reduced activity when ERGIC is removed.

claim: SEC22B-positive immunoisolated membranes have substantially increased lipidation activity (about twofold) compared to total input membrane.
source: In both experiments, the immunoisolated membranes had substantially increased activity (about twofold or more than fivefold in the SEC22B or KDELR immunoisolated membranes, respectively) compared to the total input membrane (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative comparison in Figure 8B.

claim: KDELR-positive immunoisolated membranes have substantially increased lipidation activity (more than fivefold) compared to total input membrane.
source: In both experiments, the immunoisolated membranes had substantially increased activity (about twofold or more than fivefold in the SEC22B or KDELR immunoisolated membranes, respectively) compared to the total input membrane (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative comparison in Figure 8C.

claim: Immunoisolation of lysosomes does not enrich lipidation activity compared to total input membrane.
source: In contrast, immunoisolation of lysosomes, plasma membrane/endosomes or ER did not enrich the lipidation activity compared to the total input membrane (Figure 8D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 8D.

claim: Immunoisolation of plasma membrane/endosomes does not enrich lipidation activity compared to total input membrane.
source: In contrast, immunoisolation of lysosomes, plasma membrane/endosomes or ER did not enrich the lipidation activity compared to the total input membrane (Figure 8D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 8E.

claim: Immunoisolation of ER does not enrich lipidation activity compared to total input membrane.
source: In contrast, immunoisolation of lysosomes, plasma membrane/endosomes or ER did not enrich the lipidation activity compared to the total input membrane (Figure 8D,E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 8F.

claim: ERGIC is the most active membrane substrate for LC3 lipidation.
source: Therefore the data suggest that ERGIC is the most active membrane substrate for LC3 lipidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoisolation experiments showing ERGIC enrichment correlates with highest activity.

claim: Starvation induces recruitment of ATG14 to mitochondrial-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes (MAM).
source: A recent report suggested that starvation induces the recruitment of ATG14 to a zone of adhesion between the ER and mitochondria, termed mitochondrial-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes (MAM; Hamasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is reported in a cited study by Hamasaki et al.

claim: MAM isolated by the protocol of Wieckowski et al. contains little lipidation activity.
source: Markers of this adhesion were separated from the ERGIC fraction and the adhesion membrane isolated by the protocol of Wieckowski et al. (Wieckowski et al., 2009) contained little lipidation activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting this membrane alone may not be the direct template for LC3 lipidation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activity measurements in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MAM alone may not be the direct template for LC3 lipidation.
source: Markers of this adhesion were separated from the ERGIC fraction and the adhesion membrane isolated by the protocol of Wieckowski et al. (Wieckowski et al., 2009) contained little lipidation activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting this membrane alone may not be the direct template for LC3 lipidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the low lipidation activity of MAM fractions shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A fraction of ATG14 appears on MAM in a starvation-stimulated manner.
source: Consistent with Hamasaki et al., a fraction of ATG14 appeared on MAM in a starvation-stimulated manner (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H89 is a protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor that blocks COPII-coated vesicle assembly by preventing SAR1 binding to ER membrane when used at a high concentration.
source: H89 is a protein kinase A (PKA) inhibitor that blocks COPII-coated vesicle assembly by preventing SAR1 binding to ER membrane when used at a high concentration (Chijiwa et al., 1990; Aridor and Balch, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about H89 supported by literature citations.

claim: Brefeldin A (BFA) is a fungal metabolite that inhibits ARF1 activation.
source: Brefeldin A (BFA) is a fungal metabolite that inhibits ARF1 activation (Peyroche et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BFA supported by a literature citation.

claim: Treatment of cells with 100 µM H89 leads to dispersal of ERGIC53 while GM130 remains in the perinuclear region.
source: Treatment of cells with a high concentration of H89 (100 µM) led to the dispersal of ERGIC53 whereas GM130, a cis-Golgi marker, remained in the perinuclear region, suggesting that the ERGIC is disrupted but not the cis-Golgi (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of cells with 10 µM H89 does not affect the localization of ERGIC53 or GM130.
source: A low concentration of H89 (10 µM), which is enough to inhibit PKA, did not affect the localization of either ERGIC53 or GM130 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: BFA treatment collapses the Golgi into puncta colocalizing with ERGIC53.
source: BFA treatment collapsed the Golgi into puncta colocalizing with ERGIC53 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of cells with 100 µM H89 after BFA treatment disperses both ERGIC53 and GM130.
source: Treatment of cells with 100 µM H89 after BFA treatment dispersed both ERGIC53 and GM130 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Membranes from cells treated with 100 µM H89 lose the ability to activate LC3 lipidation.
source: Membrane from cells treated with a high but not a low concentration of H89 (100 µM vs 10 µM) lost the ability to activate LC3 lipidation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9A.

claim: Membranes from cells treated with 10 µM H89 retain the ability to activate LC3 lipidation.
source: Membrane from cells treated with a high but not a low concentration of H89 (100 µM vs 10 µM) lost the ability to activate LC3 lipidation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9A.

claim: Membranes from BFA-treated cells do not show diminished lipidation activity.
source: Membranes from BFA-treated cells did not show diminished lipidation activity, nor did BFA mitigate or enhance the effect of H89 treatment on lipidation activity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9A.

claim: BFA does not mitigate or enhance the effect of H89 treatment on lipidation activity.
source: Membranes from BFA-treated cells did not show diminished lipidation activity, nor did BFA mitigate or enhance the effect of H89 treatment on lipidation activity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9A.

claim: Clofibrate is a peroxisome-proliferator activated receptor (PPAR) agonist that inhibits ER-to-Golgi transport.
source: Clofibrate is a peroxisome-proliferator activated receptor (PPAR) agonist that inhibits ER-to-Golgi transport and promotes retrograde transport of Golgi vesicles back to the ER through an unknown mechanism independent of PPAR activation (de Figueiredo and Brown, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about clofibrate supported by a literature citation.

claim: Clofibrate promotes retrograde transport of Golgi vesicles back to the ER through an unknown mechanism independent of PPAR activation.
source: Clofibrate is a peroxisome-proliferator activated receptor (PPAR) agonist that inhibits ER-to-Golgi transport and promotes retrograde transport of Golgi vesicles back to the ER through an unknown mechanism independent of PPAR activation (de Figueiredo and Brown, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about clofibrate supported by a literature citation.

claim: Clofibrate treatment leads to dispersal of ERGIC53 and GM130.
source: Clofibrate treatment led to the dispersal of ERGIC53 and GM130 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Membranes from clofibrate-treated cells fail to promote LC3 lipidation.
source: Like H89, membranes from clofribate-treated cells failed to promote LC3 lipidation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9B.

claim: kbNB142-70, a PKD inhibitor, has no effect on LC3 lipidation.
source: As controls, kbNB142-70, a PKD inhibitor (Bravo-Altamirano et al., 2011), had no affect and Pitstop 2, a clathrin inhibitor (von Kleist et al., 2011), only moderately decreased in vitro LC3 lipidation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9B.

claim: Pitstop 2, a clathrin inhibitor, only moderately decreases in vitro LC3 lipidation.
source: As controls, kbNB142-70, a PKD inhibitor (Bravo-Altamirano et al., 2011), had no affect and Pitstop 2, a clathrin inhibitor (von Kleist et al., 2011), only moderately decreased in vitro LC3 lipidation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9B.

claim: Retrograde transport to the ER requires microtubules.
source: Retrograde transport to the ER requires microtubules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about intracellular transport.

claim: Disruption of microtubules by nocodazole inhibits retrograde transport of ERGIC53 towards ER induced by H89 or clofibrate.
source: Disruption of microtubules by nocodazole inhibited the retrograde transport of ERGIC53 towards ER induced by H89 or clofibrate, preserving its punctate localization (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibitory effects of H89 and clofibrate on lipidation are reversed by nocodazole treatment.
source: Correspondingly, the inhibitory effects of H89 and clofibrate were reversed in respect to the cell-free lipidation activity (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipidation assay data in Figure 9C.

claim: ERGIC53 puncta begin to reappear within 2 min after washing out BFA and H89.
source: ERGIC53 puncta began to reappear within 2 min and the normal localization was fully restored by 20 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course immunofluorescence data in Figure 9D.

claim: Normal ERGIC53 localization is fully restored by 20 min after washing out BFA and H89.
source: ERGIC53 puncta began to reappear within 2 min and the normal localization was fully restored by 20 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course immunofluorescence data in Figure 9D and quantification in Figure 9F.

claim: Cis-Golgi regeneration is slower than ERGIC recovery and is completed by about 30 min after washing out BFA and H89.
source: Cis-Golgi regeneration, indicated by the perinuclear accumulation of GM130, was slower and was completed by about 30 min (Figure 9D,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course immunofluorescence data in Figure 9D and quantification in Figure 9F.

claim: Cell-free LC3 lipidation activity displays a rapid return correlating with the kinetics of ERGIC recovery.
source: Aliquots examined in the cell-free LC3 lipidation assay displayed a rapid return of activity correlating with the kinetics of ERGIC recovery (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course lipidation assay data in Figure 9E and correlation analysis in Figure 9F.

claim: Starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation is abolished by 100 µM H89.
source: Starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation was abolished by H89 (100 µM) and clofibrate (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10A and quantification in Figure 10B.

claim: Starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation is abolished by clofibrate.
source: Starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation was abolished by H89 (100 µM) and clofibrate (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10A and quantification in Figure 10B.

claim: Depressed formation of LC3 puncta by H89 or clofibrate is not due to enhanced autophagosome turnover.
source: Depressed formation of LC3 puncta was not due to enhanced autophagosome turnover because chloroquine, which blocks a late step in autophagy (Klionsky et al., 2012), did not mitigate the effect of H89 (100 µM) or clofibrate (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of rescue with chloroquine treatment shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: Chloroquine blocks a late step in autophagy.
source: Depressed formation of LC3 puncta was not due to enhanced autophagosome turnover because chloroquine, which blocks a late step in autophagy (Klionsky et al., 2012), did not mitigate the effect of H89 (100 µM) or clofibrate (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: Puncta formation of ATG16 is blocked by ERGIC depletion.
source: Puncta formation of another phagophore marker, ATG16 (Fujita et al., 2008), was also blocked by ERGIC depletion (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells treated with 10 µM H89 show a moderate increase in LC3 puncta with or without chloroquine.
source: In contrast to the effect of a high concentration of H89 (100 µM), cells treated with the low concentration (10 µM) showed a moderate increase in LC3 puncta with or without chloroquine (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10A and quantification in Figure 10B.

claim: PKA inhibition promotes autophagy.
source: A recent study also reported that PKA inhibition promotes autophagy (Cherra et al., 2010), thus PKA inhibition appears not to be the basis of the effect of H89 on autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: PKA inhibition is not the basis of the effect of H89 on autophagy.
source: A recent study also reported that PKA inhibition promotes autophagy (Cherra et al., 2010), thus PKA inhibition appears not to be the basis of the effect of H89 on autophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that low H89 (which inhibits PKA) increases autophagy while high H89 (which disrupts ERGIC) decreases it.

claim: A GTP-bound mutant of SAR1A (H79G) locks COPII membrane cargos on the ERES.
source: A GTP-bound mutant of SAR1A (H79G) locks COPII membrane cargos on the ERES and a GDP-bound mutant, SAR1A T34N, completely blocks COPII coat formation (Ward et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAR1A mutants supported by a literature citation.

claim: A GDP-bound mutant of SAR1A (T34N) completely blocks COPII coat formation.
source: A GTP-bound mutant of SAR1A (H79G) locks COPII membrane cargos on the ERES and a GDP-bound mutant, SAR1A T34N, completely blocks COPII coat formation (Ward et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAR1A mutants supported by a literature citation.

claim: Overexpression of SAR1A H79G leads to dispersed ERGIC53 localization.
source: Overexpression of either SAR1A H79G or T34N led to dispersed ERGIC53 localization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2) and inhibited starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation in both control and chloroquine-treated cells (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of SAR1A T34N leads to dispersed ERGIC53 localization.
source: Overexpression of either SAR1A H79G or T34N led to dispersed ERGIC53 localization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2) and inhibited starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation in both control and chloroquine-treated cells (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of SAR1A H79G or T34N inhibits starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation in both control and chloroquine-treated cells.
source: Overexpression of either SAR1A H79G or T34N led to dispersed ERGIC53 localization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2) and inhibited starvation-induced LC3 puncta formation in both control and chloroquine-treated cells (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 10C and quantification in Figure 10D.

claim: The ERGIC is a precursor of or contributes to the formation of the autophagosome.
source: We conclude that the ERGIC is a precursor of or contributes to the formation of the autophagosome.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on the genetic and pharmacological disruption experiments showing ERGIC is required for autophagosome formation.

claim: ATG14 is the key mediator bridging upstream cytosolic signals and the autophagic membrane reorganization response.
source: ATG14 is the key mediator bridging upstream cytosolic signals and the autophagic membrane reorganization response.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATG14 function in autophagy.

claim: Upon starvation, ATG14 is recruited to a membrane along with the rest of the class III PI3K complex to generate PI3P.
source: Upon starvation, ATG14 is recruited to a membrane along with the rest of the class III PI3K complex to generate PI3P (Matsunaga et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2008; Zhong et al., 2009; Matsunaga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: ATG14 and DFCP1 recruitment can be visualized by localization to puncta in starved cells.
source: These events can be visualized by the localization of ATG14 and DFCP1 to puncta in starved cells (Axe et al., 2008; Matsunaga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: 100 µM H89 prevents the formation of both ATG14 and DFCP1 puncta in starved cells.
source: As shown in Figure 11, 100 µM H89 but not 10 µM H89 prevented the formation of both ATG14 and DFCP1 puncta (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 11A and quantification in Figure 11B.

claim: 10 µM H89 does not prevent the formation of ATG14 and DFCP1 puncta in starved cells.
source: As shown in Figure 11, 100 µM H89 but not 10 µM H89 prevented the formation of both ATG14 and DFCP1 puncta (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 11A and quantification in Figure 11B.

claim: Expression of SAR1A mutants H79G and T34N inhibits ATG14 and DFCP1 puncta formation in starved cells.
source: Similar inhibition was also observed in starved cells expressing the two SAR1A mutants, H79G and T34N (Figure 11C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 11C and quantification in Figure 11D.

claim: Tagged ATG14 and DFCP1 are recruited to a buoyant membrane fraction from untreated but much less from H89-treated cells.
source: We observed recruitment of tagged ATG14 and DFCP1 to a buoyant membrane fraction from untreated but much less from H89-treated cells (Figure 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flotation assay data in Figure 12A and quantification in Figure 12B.

claim: ATG14 and DFCP1 recruitment to membranes is dependent on membranes.
source: Recruitment was dependent on membranes, and stimulated by starvation (Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flotation assay data in Figure 12—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ATG14 and DFCP1 recruitment to membranes is stimulated by starvation.
source: Recruitment was dependent on membranes, and stimulated by starvation (Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flotation assay data in Figure 12—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In starved cells, ATG14 acts upstream of PI3K activity.
source: In starved cells, ATG14 acts upstream of PI3K activity whereas DFCP1 puncta formation requires PI3P generation (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: DFCP1 puncta formation requires PI3P generation.
source: In starved cells, ATG14 acts upstream of PI3K activity whereas DFCP1 puncta formation requires PI3P generation (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: Membranes from cells treated with PI3K inhibitors recruit ATG14 but not DFCP1.
source: Correspondingly, membranes from cells treated with PI3K inhibitors recruited ATG14 but not DFCP1 (Figure 12—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flotation assay data in Figure 12—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: ATG14 and DFCP1 colocalize with ERGIC53 after starvation.
source: In addition to the membrane recruitment result, immunofluorescence studies showed colocalization of ATG14 and DFCP1 with ERGIC53 after starvation (Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the colocalization immunofluorescence data in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ERGIC membrane is an early site for the assembly of proteins responsible for the formation of the phagophore membrane.
source: We conclude that the ERGIC membrane is an early site for the assembly of proteins responsible for the formation of the phagophore membrane.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on the recruitment and colocalization data for ATG14 and DFCP1 with ERGIC.

claim: The ERGIC is a membrane compartment between ER and Golgi for cargo sorting and recycling.
source: We establish a cell-free system that reflects many of the physiological and biochemical landmarks of early events in the autophagic pathway and define the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), a membrane compartment between ER and Golgi for cargo sorting and recycling (Appenzeller-Herzog and Hauri, 2006), as a key membrane determinant for autophagosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERGIC function supported by a literature citation.

claim: The ER supports PI3P-dependent formation of the omegasome, a cradle for phagophore generation and elongation.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) supports PI3P-dependent formation of the omegasome, a cradle for phagophore generation and elongation (Axe et al., 2008; Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009; Yla-Anttila et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The outer membrane of the mitochondrion may supply lipids for the phagophore and autophagosome.
source: The outer membrane of the mitochondrion may also supply lipids for the phagophore and autophagosome (Hailey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a possibility suggested by a cited study.

claim: The ER–mitochondrial junction is required for autophagosome biogenesis.
source: Recently, a study by Hamasaki et al. (Hamasaki et al., 2013) indicates the ER–mitochondrial junction as being required for autophagosome biogenesis, possibly reconciling these two origins.
evidence: This is reported in a cited study.

claim: Clathrin-coated vesicles from the plasma membrane promote phagophore expansion through the SNARE protein VAMP7 and its partner SNAREs.
source: In addition, clathrin-coated vesicles from the plasma membrane have been shown to promote phagophore expansion through the SNARE protein VAMP7 and its partner SNAREs (Ravikumar et al., 2010; Moreau et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by literature citations.

claim: ATG9-positive vesicles cycle between distinct cytoplasmic compartments to deliver membrane to a developing autophagosome.
source: Moreover, ATG9-positive vesicles cycle between distinct cytoplasmic compartments to deliver membrane to a developing autophagosome or, in yeast, to phagophore assembly sites (PAS) (Young et al., 2006; Sekito et al., 2009; Mari et al., 2010; Nair et al., 2011; Orsi et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Autophagosomes may acquire membrane from Golgi.
source: Autophagosomes may also acquire membrane from other sources including Golgi (Geng et al., 2010; Ohashi and Munro, 2010; Yen et al., 2010; van der Vaart et al., 2010), early endosomes (Longatti et al., 2012) and vesicles budding from the ER and Golgi (Hamasaki et al., 2003; Zoppino et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a possibility supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Autophagosomes may acquire membrane from early endosomes.
source: Autophagosomes may also acquire membrane from other sources including Golgi (Geng et al., 2010; Ohashi and Munro, 2010; Yen et al., 2010; van der Vaart et al., 2010), early endosomes (Longatti et al., 2012) and vesicles budding from the ER and Golgi (Hamasaki et al., 2003; Zoppino et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a possibility supported by a literature citation.

claim: Autophagosomes may acquire membrane from vesicles budding from the ER and Golgi.
source: Autophagosomes may also acquire membrane from other sources including Golgi (Geng et al., 2010; Ohashi and Munro, 2010; Yen et al., 2010; van der Vaart et al., 2010), early endosomes (Longatti et al., 2012) and vesicles budding from the ER and Golgi (Hamasaki et al., 2003; Zoppino et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a possibility supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: A direct functional link between a membrane source and autophagosome biogenesis has not been established.
source: Although tremendous progress has been made, a direct functional link between a membrane source and autophagosome biogenesis has not been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The identity of the membrane determinant that responds to a stress signal to initiate autophagosome formation is unknown.
source: Furthermore, the identity of the membrane determinant that responds to a stress signal to initiate autophagosome formation is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: In vitro LC3 lipidation has been reconstituted with synthetic liposomes, recombinant LC3 and other components including the ATG12–ATG5 conjugate, ATG7 and ATG3.
source: In vitro LC3 lipidation has recently been reconstituted with synthetic liposomes, recombinant LC3 and other components including the ATG12–ATG5 conjugate, ATG7 and ATG3 (Sou et al., 2006; Hanada et al., 2007; Oh-oka et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2007; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about previous reconstitution systems supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The tubular and curved structure of the ERGIC in mammalian cells may favor recruitment of the ATG14 complex.
source: Perhaps the tubular and curved structure of the ERGIC (Appenzeller-Herzog and Hauri, 2006) in mammalian cells favors recruitment of the ATG14 complex and subsequently of other components.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about why ERGIC is used for autophagosome formation.

claim: ATG14 has an amphipathic alpha helix located in a C-terminal 'BATS' domain that senses membrane curvature.
source: ATG14 has been reported to sense membrane curvature via an amphipathic alpha helix located in a C-terminal 'BATS' domain (Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: In yeast, highly curved membranes positive for ATG9 are delivered to the PAS.
source: In yeast, it has been shown that highly curved membranes positive for ATG9 are delivered to the PAS (Mari et al., 2010; Nair et al., 2011; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: In yeast, the curvature sensing protein Atg1 recruits Atg13 and the Atg17–31–29 protein complex to initiate the formation of the phagophore.
source: Subsequently, the curvature sensing protein Atg1 recruits Atg13 and the Atg17–31–29 protein complex to initiate the formation of the phagophore (Ragusa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a literature citation.

claim: The ERGIC may play a role in an early stage of phagophore formation by providing a platform to recruit the class III PI3K complex.
source: Thus the ERGIC may play a role in an early stage of phagophore formation by providing a platform to recruit the class III PI3K complex and provide precursor membranes for phagophore initiation, which may be further expanded in a special subdomain of ER.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data about the role of ERGIC.

claim: The ERGIC may provide precursor membranes for phagophore initiation, which may be further expanded in a special subdomain of ER.
source: Thus the ERGIC may play a role in an early stage of phagophore formation by providing a platform to recruit the class III PI3K complex and provide precursor membranes for phagophore initiation, which may be further expanded in a special subdomain of ER.
evidence: This is the authors' speculation about how ERGIC-derived membranes might be used in phagophore formation.
